title: Anticoagulant rodenticides
why_this_matters: Anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning is among the most common toxicoses in dogs and cats, and it is treatable when recognized [3].

what_changes_from_human.point: Coagulation times can normalise within hours with IV vitamin K1, without plasma, in the retrospective series retrieved [1][3].
Response and treatment length vary with the dog and the agent, so treatment is individualized and coagulation is monitored [4].

recognition: Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticides inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, and related bleeding can be a diagnostic challenge (human review) [5].
Plasma toxin concentration at presentation varied widely in a dog series, and some dogs with characteristic coagulation disturbances and a positive response to vitamin K1 had no detectable toxin [4].
management: In 58 dogs and cats given IV lecithin-solubilised vitamin K1, no adverse effects were recorded and all had coagulation times within range by 24 hours. Survival to discharge in dogs was 96% without and 85% with exogenous coagulation factors, a difference that was not significant [1].
In 4 dogs, IV vitamin K1 normalised prothrombin time within an hour, but 2 had suspected anaphylactoid reactions and treatment stopped in one. Monitor for reactions [2].
IV mixed-micelle phytomenadione had no recorded adverse reactions in its group of dogs and cats, comparable survival and a shorter hospital stay than traditional therapy with blood products [3].
In a dog series, the vitamin K1 dose was reduced stepwise while prothrombin time stayed normal, and the authors concluded an individual approach is warranted [4].

TODO: canine vitamin K1 route, dose and treatment duration. The retrieved sources disagree on IV safety (reactions in one 4-dog series, none in two larger series) and give no canine duration for long-acting agents. Decision for the veterinary reviewer.

takeaway: Get the dog to a veterinarian, tell them the product if known, and expect coagulation to need monitoring after treatment starts.
